meta.description: Thatcher, to Woman’s Own in 1987 — and the sentence people quote is the magazine’s tidying of what the transcript records.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'There is no such thing as society'?
meta.ogDescription: Margaret Thatcher, interviewed by Douglas Keay, 23 September 1987. The transcript reads “who is society? There is no such thing!”

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.authorDates: 1925–2013 · British Conservative politician; Prime Minister of the United Kingdom, 1979–1990
answer.sourceLine: She said it, and the source is not in doubt: an interview with Douglas Keay for Woman’s Own, conducted on 23 September 1987 and published on 31 October. Wikiquote carries it in its sourced section ↗, citing the magazine at pp. 8–10. The wording is the part worth knowing about: the transcript records “and who is society? There is no such thing!”, and the sentence after it — the one about individual men and women and families — almost never survives the quotation.

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: Margaret Thatcher, interviewed by Douglas Keay
“…and who is society? There is no such thing!” — the five-word sentence is the magazine’s form

source.excerpt: I think we have gone through a period when too many children and people have been given to understand “I have a problem, it is the Government’s job to cope with it!” or “I have a problem, I will go and get a grant to cope with it!” “I am homeless, the Government must house me!” and so they are casting their problems on society and who is society? There is no such thing! There are individual men and women and there are families and no government can do anything except through people and people look to themselves first. It is our duty to look after ourselves and then also to help look after our neighbour and life is a reciprocal business and people have got the entitlements too much in mind without the obligations.
trail: Wikiquote lists the line among Thatcher’s sourced quotations ↗ — not in its Attributed, Disputed or Misattributed sections — and cites “Interview 23 September 1987, as quoted by Douglas Keay, Woman’s Own, 31 October 1987, pp. 8–10.” The same note records that the Thatcher Foundation’s transcript “differs in several particulars, but not in substance,” and that “the magazine transposed the statement in bold, often quoted out of context, from a later portion of Thatcher’s remarks.”

Wikipedia’s article on Thatcher ↗ quotes the same passage from the transcript, word for word as we print it above, and sources it to the Margaret Thatcher Foundation’s record of the interview of 23 September 1987.

Wikipedia’s article on Thatcherism ↗ cites that transcript too, and preserves a detail worth having: at the Sunday Times’s request, Number 10 issued a statement elucidating the remark, published in the ‘Atticus’ column on 10 July 1988. The sentence needed explaining within the year.

A note on what we could not do: the Margaret Thatcher Foundation’s site, which holds the full transcript, is not reachable from our fetcher, and no copy of the 1987 magazine is online. Everything above is quoted from sources we could open and read in full.
source.excerptNote: The passage as it runs in the interview transcript, printed identically by Wikiquote ↗ and Wikipedia ↗. Wikiquote adds that the magazine moved the famous sentence up from a later part of her remarks, and that the Thatcher Foundation’s transcript “differs in several particulars, but not in substance.”

author.bio: Margaret Hilda Roberts, born in Grantham in 1925, was a research chemist and then a barrister before entering the Commons as MP for Finchley in 1959. She led the Conservative Party from 1975 and was Prime Minister from 1979 to 1990. She gave this interview in September 1987, four months after winning her third general election, and spent much of the following year explaining what she had meant by it.

copyAttribution: "There is no such thing as society." — Margaret Thatcher, interviewed by Douglas Keay for Woman's Own, 23 September 1987; published 31 October 1987, pp. 8-10. In the interview transcript the words run "...they are casting their problems on society and who is society? There is no such thing! There are individual men and women and there are families..." The five-word sentence is the magazine's condensation, and the clause that follows it is almost always dropped.

misattribution.heading: How it gets quoted
misattribution.intro: The attribution is right. What goes missing is everything after the full stop.

items.who: “…who is society? There is no such thing!”
items.why: Wikipedia prints the transcript passage ↗ in which the phrase is the answer to her own rhetorical question, not a standalone declaration.

items.who: “There are individual men and women and there are families”
items.why: The clause immediately following is the one that says what she thought existed instead. It is dropped in nearly every quotation of the line, including many hostile and many admiring ones.

items.who: “There is no such thing as society” as one sentence
items.why: Wikiquote records ↗ that Woman’s Own “transposed the statement in bold… from a later portion of Thatcher’s remarks.” The five-word sentence is an editor’s arrangement of her words — an edit, not an invention.

misattribution.truthLine: She said it. She also said, in the same breath, what she thought there was instead ↗.

context.heading: Why it mattered
lead: Thatcher gave this interview on 23 September 1987, three months after winning a third term, and it became the most argued-over sentence she ever spoke — a line her critics read as the whole of her politics and her defenders read as a point about who actually does things.

The argument over it was live enough that Number 10 put out a statement explaining the remark, published in the Sunday Times in July 1988. Governments do not usually gloss a magazine interview nine months after the fact.
detailsBody: The interview transcript shows the phrase doing a different job than the quotation does. She is describing people who say “I have a problem, it is the Government’s job to cope with it”, and asks who exactly they are addressing: “who is society? There is no such thing!” The next sentence supplies her answer — individuals, and families.

Wikiquote is unusually careful about this entry, noting both that the magazine moved the sentence and that the Foundation’s transcript differs from the printed version in several particulars though not in substance. Both things can be true at once: she said it, and the form everyone knows is an editor’s.
context.pull: Not a slogan she chose. A rhetorical question, tidied into one by a magazine sub-editor.

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote carries 'There is no such thing as society' in its sourced quotations for Margaret Thatcher, citing 'Interview 23 September 1987, as quoted in by Douglas Keay, Woman's Own, 31 October 1987, pp. 8-10', notes that the Margaret Thatcher Foundation transcript 'differs in several particulars, but not in substance', and states that 'the magazine transposed the statement in bold, often quoted out of context, from a later portion of Thatcher's remarks'.

Wikipedia's Margaret Thatcher article prints the transcript passage '...and so they are casting their problems on society and who is society? There is no such thing! There are individual men and women and there are families...' and sources it to the Margaret Thatcher Foundation's record of the 23 September 1987 Woman's Own interview with Douglas Keay. It also gives her dates (13 October 1925 - 8 April 2013) and premiership (1979-1990).

Wikipedia's Thatcherism article cites the same Woman's Own interview and records that, at the Sunday Times's request, a statement elucidating the remark was issued by No.10 and published on 10 July 1988 in the 'Atticus' column.
Wikipedia describes Woman's Own as a British lifestyle magazine aimed at women, founded in 1932.
